summary: This program builds a list of farmers' market products and then uses stream pipelines to answer three questions about them: which vendors are present, what one vendor sells at what price, and what those prices would be after a 10% discount.

lines.text: Collectors supplies the ready-made recipes, such as toSet and toList, that gather a stream's results back into an ordinary collection.
The list is declared as the List interface but created as an ArrayList, so the rest of the code depends only on general list behaviour.

lines.code: products.add(new MarketProduct("Heirloom Tomatoes", "Sunny Fields Farm", 4.50, "Produce", "Summer", true));
lines.text: Each product carries a name, vendor, price, category, season, and an organic flag, which gives the stream pipelines several different fields to work with.
A Set is the right destination here because each vendor name should appear once no matter how many products that vendor sells.
Storing the vendor name in a variable means the same value drives both the menu lookup and the discount calculation.
forEach walks the finished list and hands each string to println, and the :: syntax is a method reference, a compact way of saying "call this method on each item".
Passing the discount as 0.10 rather than hard-coding it inside the method lets the same method handle any percentage.
Each task lives in its own static method, so main reads as a summary of what the program does and the stream logic stays separate.
map transforms every element into something else; here a stream of products becomes a stream of vendor names.
Filtering after the map removes missing or empty vendor names so they never reach the final set.
collect ends the pipeline and builds the actual Set, discarding duplicate vendor names automatically.
The null checks come before equalsIgnoreCase so a missing vendor cannot cause a crash, and ignoring case makes the match forgiving.
This map turns each surviving product into one display line, with %.2f forcing prices to show exactly two decimal places.
Converting the discount into a multiplier once, outside the pipeline, avoids repeating the subtraction for every product.
Math.max guards against a negative result, so an oversized discount would produce a price of zero instead of a nonsensical one.
